entries.claim: Large frame-to-frame contact changes are concentrated but not sparse: test transitions whose change magnitude d_t exceeds the training-set 90th percentile are 12.6 % (TACO), 5.7 % (ARCTIC) and 9.3 % (OakInk2) of the test transitions and hold 69.7 %, 62.4 % and 72.1 % of the summed squared change, but only 38.9 %, 29.3 % and 34.8 % of the summed unsquared change.
entries.metric: d_t = L2 norm of C_{t+1} - C_t on the raw 512-point canonical contact map (raw contact units), one value per transition (63 per 64-frame window; windows start at the first firm-contact frame). Spike = TEST transition with d_t above the 90th percentile of d_t over the TRAIN transitions of the same dataset (fixed split). Reported: fraction of test transitions that are spikes, and the fraction of sum d_t^2 ('change energy') and of sum d_t they hold. Descriptive shares, no better direction, no interval reported for them.

TACO | rounded table: spike frames (% of.locator: row dataset=TACO; columns 'spike frames (% of test transitions)', 'spike share of Σd_t² (all frames)', 'spike share of Σd_t'

caveats: The share of transitions is close to 10 % by construction: the threshold is the per-dataset TRAIN 90th percentile, so '12.6 % / 5.7 % / 9.3 % of transitions' is not a discovered sparsity; the finding is the energy share. 'Spike' means large for that dataset (thresholds 0.616 / 0.564 / 0.292 raw units), so absolute d_t is not comparable across datasets.

Squaring emphasises large changes: in unsquared magnitude the spikes hold 39 % / 29 % / 35 %, and the report's own wording is 'concentrated but not sparse' (the remaining 28-38 % of the change energy is a floor of small changes on non-spike frames).

Not every spike is a lasting reconfiguration: 46 % (TACO) and 53 % (OakInk2) of the events are low-persistence (the change cancels out within +-4 frames) against 7 % on ARCTIC, and a 3-frame moving average keeps only 28 % / 46 % of the spike energy on TACO / OakInk2 (63 % on ARCTIC). The report states it cannot decide whether these are real micro-adjustments or tracking jitter.

Test split of the fixed split only (TACO test_1; ARCTIC test; OakInk2 seeded 80/10/10 by recording); 64-frame windows that start at the first firm-contact frame; analysis of cached sequences, nothing retrained.
The report prose rounds the energy shares to 70 % / 62 % / 72 %; the tables give 0.697 / 0.624 / 0.721.

entries.claim: What the large changes are differs by dataset. By event count, TACO and OakInk2 spike events are mostly mixed or spatial-dominant (TACO 59 % and 28 % of events; OakInk2 55 % and 39 %). On ARCTIC mixed events are 48 % of the events, and firm-contact onset / release events are 26 % of the events and carry 46 % of the spike energy (wide intervals, 44 takes). At the canonical 0.7 / 0.3 cut amount-dominant events are a minority in each dataset - 4.9 % (TACO), 14.1 % (ARCTIC) and 4.7 % (OakInk2) of events, 2.8 % / 5.0 % / 1.9 % of the spike energy - but on ARCTIC that share depends on the cut (30 % of events at 0.6 / 0.4).
entries.metric: Adjacent spike transitions merged into events. Event type, in priority order: onset / release / onset+release if the event contains a firm-contact transition; otherwise amount-dominant (amount ratio r >= 0.7), spatial-dominant (r <= 0.3) or mixed, with r from the exact decomposition dC = dm * P_bar + m_bar * dP aggregated over the event. Reported: share of events (frequency) and share of the spike-frame sum d_t^2 (energy) with a take-level cluster-bootstrap 95 % interval on the energy share. Descriptive, no better direction.

TACO | mixed events: n / share of events.locator: row category=mixed; columns n_events, frequency, energy_share, energy_lo, energy_hi

TACO | onset / release / onset+release e.locator: rows category=onset, release, onset+release; columns n_events, energy_share

ARCTIC | sensitivity to the amount / spa.locator: rows dataset=ARCTIC, spike threshold=q90; column 'amount freq'

TACO | sensitivity to the amount / spati.locator: rows dataset=TACO, spike threshold=q90; columns 'amount freq', 'spatial freq', 'mixed freq'

caveats: The amount / spatial / mixed split depends on the cuts: on ARCTIC amount-dominant is 30 % of events with the looser 0.6/0.4 cut (14 % at the canonical 0.7/0.3, 2 % at 0.8/0.2); on TACO spatial moves 47 % -> 28 % -> 16 % and mixed 31 % -> 59 % -> 76 %. 'Mixed' is a residual class between two cuts, not a distinct kind of motion.

OakInk2's 33 % of spike energy in onset / release rests on 7 events from 1-2 recordings per class; every one of those energy intervals has a lower bound of 0.0. The report says classes below about 20 events (ARCTIC onset 17, OakInk2 onset / release) are reported but not interpreted.

Low-persistence is a descriptive cut that overlaps the types (not a type); no dataset shows a natural threshold in the persistence distribution, and persistence at h = 4 is undefined for events near the window edges (counted as not low-persistence in these shares).

The decomposition needs contact mass on both sides, so release-side transitions carry an amount-like change that the taxonomy labels onset / release rather than amount; one ARCTIC event (near_zero) has no valid decomposition.
Wide intervals on ARCTIC (44 takes) and OakInk2 (34 recordings).
entries.claim_as_extracted: What the large changes are differs by dataset: on TACO and OakInk2 most spike events are mixed or spatial-dominant (TACO 59 % and 28 % of events, OakInk2 55 % and 39 %), whereas on ARCTIC firm-contact onset / release events are 26 % of the events and carry 46 % of the spike energy; amount-dominant events are a small class everywhere (4.9 % / 14.1 % / 4.7 % of events).
entries.correction_reason: Numbers verified (event_summary.csv, summary_table.csv, threshold_sensitivity_all.csv). 'A small class everywhere' is loose for ARCTIC: 14.1 % of events is more than ARCTIC's spatial-dominant class (11.7 %) and becomes 30 % at the looser cut, which the extractor only says in a caveat. Missing caveat: on TACO and OakInk2 most spatial-dominant and mixed events are low-persistence among events with a defined h=4 window (event_summary.csv low_persistence_frac_defined: TACO spatial 0.752, mixed 0.553; OakInk2 spatial 0.737, mixed 0.603; ARCTIC 0.212, 0.063), so 'reconfiguration' is not a supported name for them. The report's not-interpreted list also contains OakInk2 amount (24 events), which the extractor's caveat dropped.

entries.claim: On spike frames the evolved model (B1: learned vector field rolled out from the ground-truth first map) stays close to the static baseline B0 in mean temporal error (B0 -> B1, lower is better: TACO 0.980 -> 0.917, ARCTIC 0.867 -> 0.803, OakInk2 0.533 -> 0.525). Spatial-dominant frames are essentially unchanged in all three datasets (0.972 -> 0.962, 0.811 -> 0.820, 0.485 -> 0.484). On TACO the largest reduction is on amount-dominant frames (0.877 -> 0.685, 107 frames, per-model intervals disjoint) and mixed frames are also lower (0.992 -> 0.917, intervals barely disjoint). On ARCTIC the amount (0.726 -> 0.646), onset (1.029 -> 0.942), release (0.943 -> 0.847) and mixed (0.825 -> 0.763) reductions are of similar size and all lie inside overlapping per-model intervals; on OakInk2 the point estimates are amount 0.453 -> 0.397 (34 frames from 8 recordings, a class the report does not interpret) and mixed 0.487 -> 0.473.
entries.metric: Mean temporal error e_t = L2 norm of (predicted frame-to-frame change - ground-truth change), raw contact units, lower is better, averaged over the test transitions of a frame class; for B0 (hold the ground-truth first map) e_t = d_t by construction. Frame classes = spike frames grouped by the type of their event (plus non-spike / all spike / low-persistence). Brackets: take-level cluster-bootstrap 95 % interval per model (percentiles 2.5 / 97.5; script default 500 resamples), not a paired test.

ARCTIC | release frames (n=180): tempora.locator: row frame_class=release; columns e_B0_static(_lo,_hi), e_B1_gtinit_vf(_lo,_hi), abs_B0_static, abs_B1_gtinit_vf

caveats: Corrects the wanted wording: the per-class comparison is on SPIKE frames, so 'amount' here means large changes that are mostly a change of total contact mass - not slow evolution. Mixed frames are not untouched (lower on TACO and ARCTIC); the class that is unchanged everywhere is spatial-dominant.

No paired B1-vs-B0 test exists in this thread; the intervals are per model. Only TACO all-spike, TACO amount and TACO mixed (by 0.003) have disjoint B0 / B1 intervals; TACO onset and every ARCTIC and OakInk2 per-class difference lie inside overlapping intervals.
The amount-dominant class is small: 107 / 51 / 34 frames (72 / 40 / 24 events), 3 % / 5 % / 2 % of the spike energy. On TACO amount frames B1 still leaves 0.685 of the static 0.877.

B1 starts from the GROUND-TRUTH first map, so it isolates the evolution stage; it is not the full generative pipeline. B2 / B3 (sampled first map + vector field, best-of-10 selected against the ground truth for reconstruction) are within about 0.01 of B1 on the main classes and are in the notes file.

Report prose says 'within 7 % of static on spike frames'; the ARCTIC table pair 0.867 -> 0.803 is slightly more than 7 % (own arithmetic from the two table values), OakInk2 0.533 -> 0.525 is about 1.5 %.

On ARCTIC release frames the temporal error falls (0.943 -> 0.847) while the absolute error rises (2.01 -> 2.89); the report reads this as the map changing at the right time by the wrong amount / place.
OakInk2 onset (19 frames, 1 recording) and release (59 frames, 2 recordings) have degenerate or very wide intervals and are not interpreted.
entries.claim_as_extracted: On spike frames the evolved model (B1: learned vector field rolled out from the ground-truth first map) stays close to the static baseline in temporal error (TACO 0.980 -> 0.917, ARCTIC 0.867 -> 0.803, OakInk2 0.533 -> 0.525); by event class the largest reduction is on amount-dominant frames (TACO 0.877 -> 0.685), spatial-dominant frames are unchanged in all three datasets (0.972 -> 0.962, 0.811 -> 0.820, 0.485 -> 0.484), and mixed frames lie in between (0.992 -> 0.917, 0.825 -> 0.763, 0.487 -> 0.473).
entries.correction_reason: All values verified in <ds>/model_error_by_event.csv. 'The largest reduction is on amount-dominant frames' is established for TACO only: on ARCTIC the largest absolute reduction is on release frames (0.095) then onset (0.087) then amount (0.080), all with overlapping intervals; on OakInk2 it is a point estimate on a not-interpreted class. Intervals are per model (take-level bootstrap), no paired test exists. Otherwise direction and strength are right, and the wording avoids 'predicts sliding'.

entries.claim: Averaged over all test transitions the evolved model's mean temporal error is not lower than the static baseline's (static B0 -> evolved B1: TACO 0.317 -> 0.318, ARCTIC 0.167 -> 0.194, OakInk2 0.142 -> 0.144), and most of B1's summed (unsquared) temporal error lies on non-spike frames (64 % / 77 % / 66 %). Spike frames hold 36 % / 23 % / 34 % of it; among them mixed plus spatial-dominant frames are the largest part on TACO (21 % + 10 %) and OakInk2 (16 % + 10 %), while on ARCTIC it is mixed (10 %) and release (7 %) frames, with spatial-dominant frames at 3 %.
entries.metric: (a) mean temporal error e_t over all / non-spike test transitions (lower is better, take-level cluster-bootstrap 95 % interval); (b) share of a model's summed e_t (unsquared) that falls in a frame class (descriptive); (c) mean absolute error |C_hat_t - C_t| at the same frames (lower is better).

caveats: This corrects the block headline: the summed temporal error is NOT concentrated in spatial / mixed transitions - 64-77 % of B1's sum e_t is on non-spike frames, where its error is at or above the 'no change' floor (ARCTIC 0.125 -> 0.157). What the tables support is that the per-frame error is several times higher on spike frames and that, within spike frames, the spatial-dominant class is left unchanged.
The shares are of the unsquared sum e_t; no squared-error share is reported for the models, so they are not directly comparable with the 62-72 % share of sum d_t^2.

The 'slow evolution' statement is separate and TACO-only: the report attributes B1's TACO gain in ABSOLUTE error (3.42 -> 1.77 on non-spike frames) to 'the slow amount trend accumulated below the spike threshold'. That attribution is the report's interpretation, not a separately tested result, and there is no comparable absolute gain on ARCTIC (2.20 -> 2.12) or OakInk2 (1.25 -> 1.24).
On ARCTIC B1's temporal error is higher than static on non-spike frames and on all frames; the two intervals overlap only marginally on non-spike frames (B0 upper 0.1417, B1 lower 0.1403).

BimArt (B4, TACO and ARCTIC only) is in the notes file and not in the figure: its 'own support' error is not like-for-like with B0 / B1, and on TACO it is the project's own gen3 port trained on the same split (ARCTIC: BimArt's pretrained contact model).
entries.claim_as_extracted: Averaged over all test transitions the evolved model's temporal error is not lower than the static baseline's (TACO 0.317 vs 0.318, ARCTIC 0.167 vs 0.194, OakInk2 0.142 vs 0.144), and most of its summed temporal error lies on non-spike frames (64 % / 77 % / 66 %); spike frames hold 36 % / 23 % / 34 % of it, of which mixed plus spatial frames are the largest part on TACO (21 % + 10 %) and OakInk2 (16 % + 10 %).
entries.correction_reason: Values verified (row 'all', row 'non_spike', column e_B1_gtinit_vf_share_of_total). The parenthesis lists static first and evolved second while the sentence names the evolved model first, so 'TACO 0.317 vs 0.318' can be read the wrong way round; label the order. ARCTIC's within-spike split was left out although it differs (mixed 0.098, release 0.067, spatial 0.027). One attached caveat mixes frame classes: 'no comparable absolute gain on ARCTIC (2.20 -> 2.12) or OakInk2 (1.25 -> 1.24)' quotes ALL-frame values next to TACO's NON-SPIKE value (3.42 -> 1.77); the like-for-like non-spike values are ARCTIC 2.20 -> 2.11 and OakInk2 1.13 -> 1.14.

entries.claim: In the report's documented TACO example (a knife in a cutting take, one test sequence) the evolved model's mean temporal error is below the static baseline's (which equals the ground-truth change) on the amount-dominant event at transitions 7-8 (0.593 vs 0.726) and close to it on the representative spatial-dominant event at 34-35 (0.813 vs 0.792) and on the large mixed event at 39-42 (1.921 vs 2.014). In the same sequence it is above the static baseline on another spatial-dominant event at 19-20 (1.261 vs 0.673) and below it on a mixed event at 26-28 (0.542 vs 0.860). A single illustrative sequence, consistent with the per-class averages but carrying no statistical weight.

entries.claim: Where hand-surface motion was measured (TACO and ARCTIC; not OakInk2), the contact change magnitude d_t is associated with the hand's speed relative to the object at the same transition: Spearman 0.785 [0.767, 0.801] on TACO with the corrected tool-frame transform (0.675 [0.650, 0.694] as originally published) and 0.513 [0.413, 0.621] on ARCTIC. In each of these two datasets the association is stronger than with the other signals measured there: on TACO object linear / angular speed 0.199 / 0.197 and tool-versus-target linear / angular speed 0.111 / 0.142; on ARCTIC object linear / angular speed 0.014 / 0.177 and articulation rate 0.026. OakInk2 has no hand signal; its object linear / angular speed correlations are 0.167 / 0.333. This is a same-transition association, not a prediction result.
entries.metric: Spearman rank correlation over all test transitions between d_t and a per-frame kinematic signal of the same transition; bracket = take-level cluster-bootstrap 95 % interval (200 resamples). Hand-relative speed = mean over the 100 sampled hand-surface points of the frame-to-frame displacement in the object's canonical frame (m/frame). An association (no better direction), not a prediction score.

caveats: Which value is which: 0.675 (prose 0.68) is the temporal-event report's published TACO value, computed with a wrong reading of the tool-frame 6D rotation on tool-role sequences; 0.785 (INDEX.md: 0.79) is the corrected value from the follow-up study's sanity file. The correction strengthens the association; target-role sequences and ARCTIC are unaffected.

The bug is not fixed in the temporal-event thread: its script, its tables (kinematic_associations*.csv, the frames_test.csv hand column, event_type_table.csv hand column), its Figure E and its report text still carry the uncorrected TACO hand numbers. TACO's Cliff's delta (0.70) and hand-speed medians (0.0032 -> 0.0100 m/frame) were not recomputed with the corrected transform in any source read here, so quote only the Spearman value for TACO.

An association between two quantities of the same transition, not a prediction result and not a causal one; the follow-up study (block F1-subB) concluded that hand and contact transitions are 'strongly coupled but mostly simultaneous'.
Hand-surface motion was measured on TACO and ARCTIC only; OakInk2 has no hand signal. Articulation exists only for ARCTIC, tool-versus-target motion only for TACO.

Object motion is weakly, not zero, associated: OakInk2's object angular speed has Spearman 0.333 [0.237, 0.444], and on TACO the median object / tool speeds are higher during spatial and mixed events than on non-spike frames (kinematic_associations_all.csv). On TACO 'object speed' is the target object's world speed for every sequence, including tool-role sequences whose contacted object is the tool.

The report states that hand-tracking jitter and real micro-adjustments would both raise the hand-relative speed, so the association does not show that the co-occurring spikes are physical contact changes.
Frame-level correlations are exploratory; uncertainty is clustered by take (186 / 44 / 34 clusters), hence the wide ARCTIC interval.
entries.claim_as_extracted: Where hand-surface motion was measured, the contact change magnitude d_t is associated with the hand's speed relative to the object at the same transition (Spearman 0.785 [0.767, 0.801] on TACO with the corrected tool-frame transform, 0.675 [0.650, 0.694] as originally published; 0.513 [0.413, 0.621] on ARCTIC), and more strongly than with object linear or angular speed (0.01 to 0.33), tool-versus-target motion (0.11 to 0.14) or ARCTIC's articulation rate (0.03).
entries.correction_reason: All values verified. The pooled range '0.01 to 0.33' takes its upper end from OakInk2 (object angular speed 0.333), a dataset with no hand signal, so 'hand more strongly than object (0.33)' compares across datasets; the page rule is per dataset. Which value is which is right: 0.785 (INDEX.md 0.79) is the corrected one, 0.675 (prose 0.68) the published one. 'Is associated with' is allowed wording; 'strongly' fits TACO, ARCTIC's 0.513 has a wide interval (44 takes). Attached caveats (simultaneous coupling in the follow-up study, jitter cannot be told from micro-adjustment, TACO Cliff's delta and medians not recomputed) are accurate.

dataset_differences: Spike share of transitions and of squared change: TACO 12.6 % -> 69.7 %, ARCTIC 5.7 % -> 62.4 %, OakInk2 9.3 % -> 72.1 % (unsquared: 38.9 % / 29.3 % / 34.8 %). Thresholds are per dataset (train Q90 = 0.616 / 0.564 / 0.292 raw units), so shares and shapes are comparable, absolute d_t is not.
Event density: 4.02 (TACO), 1.52 (ARCTIC), 2.54 (OakInk2) merged spike events per 64-frame sequence (1464 / 283 / 510 test events).

Event types: TACO and OakInk2 are mostly mixed + spatial-dominant (TACO 59.4 % + 28.2 % of events, 61.5 % + 23.7 % of spike energy; OakInk2 55.1 % + 38.8 %, 40.4 % + 25.1 %). ARCTIC: onset / release family 26 % of events and 46 % of spike energy (release alone 19.1 % / 31.6 %), mixed 48.1 % / 39.0 %, spatial 11.7 % / 9.5 %. OakInk2 has only 7 onset / release events, which nevertheless carry 33 % of the spike energy (intervals reach 0).
Amount-dominant events: 4.9 % (TACO), 14.1 % (ARCTIC), 4.7 % (OakInk2) of events; 2.8 % / 5.0 % / 1.9 % of spike energy. On ARCTIC the share rises to 30 % of events with the looser 0.6/0.4 cut.

Persistence: TACO and OakInk2 spikes are largely transient (46 % / 53 % of events low-persistence; a 3-frame moving average keeps 28 % / 46 % of the spike energy), ARCTIC spikes are persistent (7 % low-persistence; 63 % kept).

Evolved model vs static on spike frames: TACO 0.980 -> 0.917 with disjoint intervals; ARCTIC 0.867 -> 0.803 with overlapping intervals; OakInk2 0.533 -> 0.525, essentially no difference. Disjoint per-class intervals exist only on TACO (all-spike, amount, mixed).
Evolved model vs static on non-spike and all frames: TACO and OakInk2 a tie (all frames 0.317 vs 0.318; 0.142 vs 0.144), ARCTIC worse (non-spike 0.125 -> 0.157, all 0.167 -> 0.194).
Absolute error: a large gain on TACO only (all frames 3.47 -> 1.81); ARCTIC 2.20 -> 2.12 with spike frames worse (2.21 -> 2.36) and release frames much worse (2.01 -> 2.89); OakInk2 1.25 -> 1.24.
Low-persistence frames: unchanged by the evolved model on TACO (1.066 -> 1.062) and OakInk2 (0.513 -> 0.512); lower on ARCTIC (0.811 -> 0.737) but that class is 35 frames from 19 events.

Hand association: TACO 0.785 (corrected; 0.675 published), ARCTIC 0.513 with a wide interval [0.413, 0.621]; OakInk2 has no hand signal. Articulation rate exists only on ARCTIC (0.026, interval spans 0; Cliff's delta -0.14), tool-vs-target motion only on TACO (0.11 / 0.14). OakInk2's strongest available signal is object angular speed (0.333).
Test-set size in independent units: TACO 364 sequences from 186 takes, ARCTIC 186 from 44 takes, OakInk2 201 from 34 recordings - ARCTIC and OakInk2 intervals are wide.

BimArt (B4) rows exist for TACO and ARCTIC only, and are different models (TACO: the project's gen3 port trained on the same split; ARCTIC: BimArt's pretrained contact model). Not used in the module's figures.
The timeline example exists for TACO and ARCTIC (described in the report text); none is described for OakInk2.
do_not_claim: 'Temporal failure (the temporal error) is concentrated in spatial / mixed transitions' as a statement about the total error: 61-77 % of every B0-B3 model's summed temporal error is on NON-spike frames (B1: 64 % / 77 % / 66 %).

'The temporal model's gains are in the slow evolution' as a per-class result: the per-class comparison is on spike frames only; on non-spike frames the evolved model's temporal error is not lower than static (ARCTIC: higher). The 'slow amount trend' reading is the report's interpretation of the TACO absolute-error gain and is TACO-only.

'The model predicts amount changes well' or 'the model perfectly predicts sliding': on TACO amount frames it still has 0.685 against 0.877 for static, and on spatial-dominant frames it is unchanged on every dataset.
'The model cannot predict any spatial or mixed change': mixed frames are lower on TACO (0.992 -> 0.917) and ARCTIC (0.825 -> 0.763).
'The evolved model beats the static baseline in temporal error': averaged over all transitions it does not (0.317 vs 0.318; 0.167 vs 0.194; 0.142 vs 0.144).
Any ARCTIC or OakInk2 per-class difference presented as significant: their B0 / B1 intervals overlap and no paired test exists in this thread.

'Only about 10 % of frames matter' or '12.6 % of frames' as a discovered sparsity: the threshold is the train 90th percentile, so the frame share is near 10 % by construction; the report's own conclusion is 'concentrated but not sparse'.
A pooled statement such as 'about 10 % of transitions hold about 70 % of the change' across datasets: report 12.6 % -> 69.7 % (TACO), 5.7 % -> 62.4 % (ARCTIC), 9.3 % -> 72.1 % (OakInk2) separately.

'Spikes are sliding / regrasp / reconfiguration events': on TACO and OakInk2 about half of the events are low-persistence oscillations that cancel within a few frames, and the report cannot tell real micro-adjustments from tracking jitter. Equally do not call them 'noise' or 'jitter' as a fact (the report's phrase 'treat the residual high-frequency part as noise' is a recommendation for a training target, not a finding).
'Contact does not move over time' or 'spatial changes are irrelevant': nothing in this thread supports either.
'Hand motion predicts (or causes, or drives) contact change': the Spearman values are same-transition associations; the follow-up study found the coupling mostly simultaneous.

'Object motion is unrelated to contact change': the correlations are weak (0.01-0.33), not zero; OakInk2's object angular speed is 0.333 and on TACO object / tool speeds are elevated during spatial and mixed events.
Quoting 0.68 as the TACO hand correlation without the correction, or quoting TACO's Cliff's delta 0.70 / 'median hand speed triples' as corrected values (they were not recomputed).
Any hand-motion statement for OakInk2 (no hand signal), or 'hand-relative speed is the strongest signal on all three datasets'.

Describing the timeline as 'ground-truth versus predicted contact change': the table holds the error of the predicted change, not its magnitude; and the two sequences are single illustrations, not typical-case statistics.
Attributing the TACO BimArt (B4) numbers to the released BimArt model, or comparing BimArt 'own support' errors with B0 / B1 as like-for-like.
Using the report's hypothesis letters (A-D): A and C are never defined in the saved files.
Presenting the report's recommendation (train on a 3-5 frame smoothed / persistent displacement) as a tested result: it was not tested in this thread.
'Amount-dominant changes are rare' as cut-independent on ARCTIC (30 % of events at the 0.6/0.4 cut).
